title: Reading the current value in the condition
idea: The if's condition uses the loop variable i, which changes each pass — so the same condition gives different answers across passes. Deepen the mental model.

exercises.prompt: Why can the SAME condition (if i > 3) act differently on different passes?
options: Because i changes each pass, so the comparison's result changes too
It can't — it's always the same
exercises.explanation: The condition reads i, and i is different each pass. So i > 3 is false early and true later.

exercises.prompt: For i in range(1, 6), on which passes is i > 3 true?
exercises.explanation: i > 3 is true for 4 and 5, false for 1, 2, 3. The same test, re-checked with each new i.
print(i) runs every pass; 'found 3' only when i == 3. The condition fires on exactly one pass.

exercises.prompt: A condition inside a loop is re-evaluated with the current value of i on every single pass.
exercises.explanation: Yes. Each pass, the if looks at the current i and decides afresh. That's why its behavior can change pass to pass.
>= includes 3, so 3, 4, 5 print. Recall: >= means 'greater than OR equal to'.

exercises.prompt: Match each condition to the i values that pass it, for i in range(1, 6).
exercises.explanation: Each condition selects a different set of passes as i walks 1 to 5. Reading the comparison predicts the set.
i > limit (3) is true for 4 and 5. The condition can compare i to a named value, not just a literal.
>= includes the limit itself, so 3, 4, 5 print. Choosing > vs >= decides whether the boundary is included.
!= means 'not equal'. Every i except 3 passes, so 1, 2, 4, 5 print. The one value where it's equal is skipped.

exercises.prompt: A learner expected if i > 3 to act on every pass. Why does it only act on some?
options: Because i is small (1, 2, 3) early and the test is false then — it only becomes true at 4
exercises.explanation: The condition depends on i, which starts small. It stays false until i grows past 3. Conditions in loops respond to the changing value.
